correctness.rationale: The zero diagonal makes P_A separately affine, so extrema reduce to 2^n sign vertices; B_A is separately affine in both vectors. Conjugating by one sign vector makes the other a U/V cut and cancels cross contributions, B=a−b. Averaging P over opposite signs on one block bounds |q_U+q_V| by M=||P||. If a cut block has ≤2 elements, its quadratic value is negatable; every n≤5 cut, and unbalanced n=6 cuts, obey |a−b|≤M. For n=6 split 3+3, each triple one-flip average is −(its all-ones value)/3, so |a−b/3|≤M and |b−a/3|≤M; subtract to get |a−b|≤3M/2. Opposite-signed complete triangles realize polynomial norm 8 and bilinear norm 12. My independently implemented exact fraction certificate checked all 16+64+256+1024+4096 sign pairs (not a sample over matrices), matching coefficient identities for arbitrary real A and maximal coefficient mass 1 or 3/2 as claimed. These finite dimension computations corroborate the universal coefficient inequalities; the analytic averaging proves the theorem.
residual_risks: Only real matrices and zero diagonal; complex/all-polynomial polarization constants differ.
No exact c_n asserted for n≥7.

value.rationale: The first dimension at which real square-free quadratic polarization ceases to preserve norm is a natural structural invariant of multi-affine polynomial geometry, not a reparametrization of unrestricted polarization. Proving complete optimal constants through the first failure and identifying a sparse exact extremizer provides useful finite-dimensional boundary data for operator/polynomial norm inequalities.
residual_risks: No claims of infinite-dimensional sharpness or higher-n classification.

final_claim: For real symmetric zero-diagonal matrices on ℓ∞^n, the square-free quadratic polarization constant equals 1 for 2≤n≤5 and equals 3/2 for n=6; padding gives c_n≥3/2 for n≥6, without claiming sharpness beyond six.
limitations: For n≥7 only a lower bound follows from padding; no upper bound above 3/2 is claimed.
Finite certificates concern n≤6 and arbitrary real coefficients by exact identities, not higher n.
